rows.name: Archer Push-Up
rows.reason: Isometric Wipers is a low side-to-side 'wiper' (typewriter) push-up, not an archer push-up. An archer rep starts at the top with both arms straight and wide, lowers toward one hand while the other arm stays straight, then presses back to lockout. The wiper pair never shows a straight-arm top. Its second frame is a centred, bent-arm position that is not part of an archer rep, so copying the two frames teaches staying low and sliding across, a different range and progression. Single-Arm_Push-Up has the free hand behind the back, so it is a one-arm push-up, not an archer. Push-Up_Wide is a symmetric wide push-up, Plyo_Kettlebell_Pushups is a kettlebell crossover, and Clock_Push-Up shows a plain push-up. A curator who treats typewriter push-ups as archer push-ups could revisit Isometric_Wipers, whose frame 0 alone is a credible archer bottom, but by the strict rule it is a near miss.

rows.name: Spiderman Push-Up
rows.reason: This is the closest candidate, but it is a different exercise. The source's own instructions say to hold the bent-arm (90 degree) position and alternate knee-to-elbow, a low-plank crawl drill. A Spiderman push-up starts with the arms straight, brings the knee to the elbow while lowering, then presses back up to lockout. The photos show no elbow extension or press, so someone copying them would do a low isometric knee-drive, not a push-up. The other candidates are wrong too: Mountain_Climbers and Groiners have arms straight and no push-up, Push_Up_to_Side_Plank is a rotation, and Pushups is a standard push-up with no knee drive, which is the base exercise for a named variation.

rows.name: Meadows Row
rows.reason: A Meadows row is a named variation of the one-arm landmine row. The lifter stands side-on to the bar in a staggered stance, braces the free forearm on the front knee, and grips the very end of the bar (the sleeve) overhand, rowing with the elbow flared. Both source photos show the standard one-arm landmine (long bar) row instead: bar running alongside the body, square stance, grip on the shaft. Under the rules, the base exercise cannot stand in for a named variation. Bent_Over_Two-Arm_Long_Bar_Row and T-Bar_Row_with_Handle are two-arm rows, so they are ruled out too.

rows.name: Cable Pullover
rows.reason: The app lists 'Cable Pullover' (#63) separately from 'Straight-Arm Cable Pulldown' (#62), and #62 already uses the Straight-Arm_Pulldown photo. That suggests #63 is the classic lying cable pullover: supine on a flat bench, arms nearly straight, arcing from behind the head to over the chest. No source shows that. The incline-bench candidate fails on two counts: the bench is a steep incline rather than flat, and the elbows bend and the bar is pulled to the chest. The standing rope and bar straight-arm pulldowns would teach a standing body position for what is probably a lying exercise. Near miss: if the app means the standing 'cable pullover' (the rope straight-arm pulldown), Rope_Straight-Arm_Pulldown would fit, with frame 0 as the start. With the app separating the two names, that is too uncertain to propose.

No source exercise uses that implement or movement. A dumbbell or barbell pullover is a different implement and a supine body position, and a machine row is a different movement. I did not view these frames because none of them can match on implement and pattern.

rows.name: Commando Pull-Up
rows.reason: In a commando pull-up the body is turned side-on to the bar, both hands grip the bar close together one in front of the other, and the head clears alternate sides of the bar. Mixed_Grip_Chin is facing the bar with shoulder-width hands, not side-on. V-Bar_Pullup uses a V-handle attachment and does not alternate sides. Side_To_Side_Chins uses a wide grip facing the bar. None of them shows the commando grip or path.

rows.name: Archer Pull-Up
rows.reason: An archer pull-up keeps the non-working arm nearly straight and extended out to the side while the other arm pulls. In Side_To_Side_Chins both arms flex and the torso only leans to one side, which is a lateral-lean wide pull-up, not an archer. The standard Pullups photo is the base exercise, which the rules forbid for a named variation. No source shows one arm locked straight.

Gorilla_Chin_Crunch uses bent knees tucked dynamically, so the trunk position and abdominal demand differ. Pullups has the legs hanging. Hanging_Leg_Raise and Hanging_Pike are leg raises with no pull-up. No source shows a pull-up with the legs held straight in an L.

Standing_Towel_Triceps_Extension is unrelated. No source shows a two-hand towel pull-up.

rows.name: Trap-Bar Shrug
rows.reason: The source has no trap-bar shrug. Trap_Bar_Deadlift uses the right implement but shows a deadlift (hips and knees extend from the floor), not scapular elevation. Barbell_Shrug, Dumbbell_Shrug, Cable_Shrugs and the machine shrugs show the right movement with the wrong implement. A barbell or dumbbell shrug is not a trap-bar shrug.

rows.name: Dumbbell Y-Raise
rows.reason: The source has no Y-raise. Scaption has the right implement and plane, but its range stops at about shoulder height (the source says until the arms are parallel to the ground), while a Y-raise finishes with the arms overhead in a Y. The app groups this exercise with rear delts and traps, which suggests the lower-trap Y-raise, usually chest-supported or bent over, not a standing front/side-delt scaption. Standing_Dumbbell_Straight-Arm_Front_Delt_Raise_Above_Head goes overhead but in the sagittal plane with the arms parallel (an I, not a Y). Reverse_Flyes_With_External_Rotation finishes in a T, and Iron_Cross is a squat plus front raise followed by a lateral raise. None show a Y.

rows.name: Cable Y-Raise
rows.reason: The source has no cable Y-raise. Both cable candidates stop at shoulder or eye height, in the frontal or sagittal plane, with no overhead Y finish. The dumbbell and barbell raises use the wrong implement.

rows.name: Prone Y-Raise
rows.reason: The prone position is right, but the movement is a barbell front raise with the arms parallel. A barbell cannot make a Y, so this is a prone I-raise, not a Y-raise. The other prone raises (Dumbbell_Lying_Rear_Lateral_Raise, Reverse_Flyes, Lying_Rear_Delt_Raise) finish in a T at shoulder level, not a Y overhead. Superman is a lower-back extension. The source has no prone Y-raise.

rows.name: Prone W-Raise
rows.reason: A W-raise is done lying face down with the elbows bent about 90 degrees and tucked toward the ribs. The athlete squeezes the shoulder blades down and back and rotates the forearms up and out so the arms form a W. Every prone candidate is a straight-arm reverse fly to a T, which is a different arm path and shape. Cuban_Press is done standing and ends in an overhead press. The source has no bent-elbow prone W.

rows.name: Scapular Wall Slide
rows.reason: I searched for wall, slide, scap and scapula in names and instructions. No source exercise has the back or forearms against a wall while the arms slide overhead and back down. Scapular_Pull-Up (a hanging depression) and Upward_Stretch (a free-standing overhead stretch) are different movements. The source has no wall slide.

rows.name: Z-Press
rows.reason: This is the only floor-seated press in the source. The standard Z-press is a two-hand press, usually with a barbell or a pair of dumbbells, done seated on the floor with the legs straight out in front and no support from the hands or a backrest. The photo is one arm with a kettlebell and straddled legs, and the free hand may be bracing on the floor. That differs from the standard version in laterality and implement, and possibly in support. Showing it for a generic Z-Press would teach a single-arm kettlebell variant. The seated bench presses (Seated_Barbell_Military_Press, Seated_Dumbbell_Press) use a bench with a backrest, which is what the Z-press removes.

rows.name: Machine Lateral Raise
rows.reason: I checked every machine exercise for a lateral raise and searched the instructions for 'lateral raise machine' with no hits. The only lateral raises use dumbbells, cables or bands, which is the wrong implement for a machine exercise. The presses and the reverse fly are different movement patterns.

'Behind the back' in the instructions appears only in unrelated exercises (a barbell shrug, rope rear-delt rows).

rows.name: Bayesian Cable Curl
rows.reason: A Bayesian curl is done facing AWAY from a low/mid pulley with the working arm drawn behind the torso (shoulder extended) so the cable pulls from behind. No source photo shows that set-up: the one-arm cable curl has the cable in front/at the side with the upper arm vertical, and the overhead/high-pulley curls are two-arm with arms abducted to the sides. Copying any of them would give a different curl.

rows.name: Chin-Up Curl
rows.reason: The app lists 'Chin-Up' (#67) separately from 'Chin-Up Curl' (#138). #138 sits in the biceps group with the movement 'Elbow flexion', so it is a named variation, a bar curl done with bodyweight. The source has no such exercise; searches for bodyweight curl or 'curl yourself' found nothing. Using the standard chin-up photo would be the base exercise for a named variation, which the rules forbid, and the app already has a chin-up entry for that photo. Gorilla_Chin_Crunch adds a knee tuck. The confidence is medium only because the exact definition of 'Chin-Up Curl' is not documented in the app catalog.

rows.name: Dead Hang
rows.reason: A dead hang is a still, passive two-arm hang, so both frames should show the same hang. In every candidate only frame 0 is a hang, and frame 1 shows a different movement (scapular pull-up, pike, chin-up). Someone copying the pair would do that movement instead of hanging. One_Handed_Hang is one-armed, keeps the feet on the floor and is a stretch. The closest is Scapular_Pull-Up, but its frame 1 is a scapular pull-up, which the app lists as its own exercise (#79).

rows.name: Towel Dead Hang
rows.reason: A towel dead hang is a still hang with both hands gripping towels looped over the bar. One_Arm_Chin-Up has one hand on the bar and one on a towel, and its frame 1 is a pull-up, not a hang. No other source mentions a towel on a hanging exercise. Plain dead-hang frames (Scapular_Pull-Up, Hanging_Pike frame 0) have no towel and are not dead hangs either (see #143).

rows.name: Farmer Hold
rows.reason: Farmer Hold is a static grip hold: stand still holding heavy implements at your sides. Farmer's Walk is the loaded-carry version; its frame 1 clearly shows walking, so someone copying it would carry, not hold. The name 'Hold' is what sets the exercise apart from the walk, so this is the base exercise standing in for a named variation. Dumbbell Shrug's frame 0 looks like the hold position, but frame 1 is a shrug, so the pair teaches shrugging. Plate Pinch and the plate squeeze use a one-hand pinch or finger grip on plates, not a two-hand farmer hold. No source shows a static two-hand farmer hold.

rows.name: Bodyweight Triceps Extension
rows.reason: Body_Tricep_Press is exactly the movement (the standard bar 'bodyweight skull crusher'), but the photos show visible added load: chains over the shoulders. The rule says 'Bodyweight' must be unloaded, so it is a near miss and is rejected. A reviewer who accepts the chains could use it, and its frame 0 (arms extended) is the rep start. Body-Up is unloaded, but it is the floor forearm-to-hands 'sphinx/tiger' variation, a different set-up from the bar/ledge bodyweight triceps extension. The app lists 'Free weights', which also suggests a bar is used. Standing_Towel_Triceps_Extension is partner-resisted with a towel overhead, not bodyweight-loaded.

rows.name: Pendulum Squat

The hack squat (linear sled), the lying machine squat (reclined press-style machine) and the barbell hack squat (barbell behind the legs) are different implements with a different movement path. Searches for 'pendulum' and 'squat machine' found nothing closer.

rows.name: Peterson Step-Up

Under the rules, the base step-up does not stand in for this named variation.

rows.name: Cyclist Squat

No source exercise shows heel elevation; an instructions search for heels on, raised or elevated, wedges or plates under the feet found nothing for squats. Narrow_Stance_Squats lacks the heel elevation that defines the exercise. The sissy squat is a different movement, a backward lean with the hips kept extended.

rows.name: Assisted Nordic Curl

No source shows the assistance that defines this variation: no band around the chest, no box or partner helping, no hand push-off during the lowering. The partner in Floor_Glute-Ham_Raise only anchors the feet, which is the standard Nordic set-up, not assistance. In Natural_Glute_Ham_Raise frame 1 the hands only catch the body at the bottom of a full Nordic. Glute_Ham_Raise is a GHD machine exercise with a different set-up. Using the base exercise for a named variation is not allowed.

rows.name: Slider Hamstring Curl
rows.reason: A slider hamstring curl is done with the hips bridged off the floor. The heels slide out and back in while the hips stay extended, which is what loads the hamstrings (the same set-up as Ball_Leg_Curl, but on sliders). This source photo is a heel slide with the hips on the floor. There is no bridge or hip extension, so the hamstrings barely work against gravity. Someone copying it would do a mobility-style heel slide, not the app's exercise. Ball_Leg_Curl uses a stability ball, a different implement, and is already app #197. No other slider or towel curl exists in the source.

Its instructions use the word 'abduct', but they describe adduction. Swapping the frames would not help: the cable pulls toward abduction, so the load opposes the wrong muscles. Thigh_Abductor shows the right action, but on a seated two-leg machine instead of a standing single-leg cable. The source has no cable abduction photo.

rows.name: Copenhagen Plank
rows.reason: A Copenhagen plank needs the top leg resting on a bench or a partner's arm while the body is held in a side plank. Side_Bridge has both feet on the floor and no elevated top leg, so it is the base side plank. The source has no exercise named or instructed as a Copenhagen or adductor plank. The adductor sources found are stretches (Adductor_Groin, Side_Lying_Groin_Stretch, Lying_Bent_Leg_Groin) or machine, cable or band adduction.

rows.name: Cossack Squat
rows.reason: This is the only lateral squat or lunge in the source, and it is a back-loaded barbell side split squat (a stationary lateral lunge) to about parallel. A Cossack squat sinks to full depth on one leg, with the straight leg's heel down and toes pointing up, and it is normally done bodyweight or front/goblet-loaded. The depth, the trailing-foot position and the barbell back load make this a lateral lunge rather than a Cossack squat. No source entry mentions a Cossack squat.

rows.name: Single-Leg Calf Raise
rows.reason: The source has no standing single-leg calf raise. The closest candidates each fail on one rule. Calf_Raise_On_A_Dumbbell is a nonstandard rolling calf raise on a dumbbell handle; its instructions never say one leg, and the free foot appears to rest on the floor, so copying it would not give a single-leg calf raise. Dumbbell_Seated_One-Leg_Calf_Raise is single-leg but seated, a soleus raise, so the body position is wrong. Every standing calf-raise photo is two-legged, so the laterality is wrong.

rows.name: Tibialis Raise
rows.reason: The source has no tibialis raise, bodyweight or wall-supported. Smith_Machine_Reverse_Calf_Raises is a Smith-machine set-up, so the implement is wrong, and the rear-view photos do not show the dorsiflexion at all. Rocking_Standing_Calf_Raise alternates a toe raise with a calf raise under a barbell. Its frame 1 is a calf raise, so copying the two frames gives a rocking calf raise, not a tibialis raise. The searches for 'tibialis', 'toe' and 'dorsi' found only SMR and stretching entries.

rows.name: Weighted Tibialis Raise
rows.reason: A weighted tibialis raise needs load on the forefoot, such as a tib bar, a plate or a dumbbell on the toes, or a band. No source shows that. In both candidates the load sits on the back, which goes through the heels and does not load dorsiflexion. The Smith source itself says the bar is only for balance. Rocking_Standing_Calf_Raise also shows a calf raise as its second frame, so its movement is wrong as well. Neither photo teaches a loaded tibialis raise.

rows.name: Toe Walk
rows.reason: The source has no toe walk or tip-toe walking drill. A stationary calf raise is a different movement pattern, not locomotion. An instructions search for 'on your toes' and 'walk on' found no gait drill.

rows.name: Heel Walk
rows.reason: The source has no heel walk. The standing toe-raise photos (Smith_Machine_Reverse_Calf_Raises and frame 0 of Rocking_Standing_Calf_Raise) are stationary, loaded on the back, and in the rocking case alternate with a calf raise. They are not a walking drill.

rows.name: Hanging Leg Raise

rows.name: L-Sit

The closest photos differ in body position and support: the captain's chair rests on the forearms with the back against a pad and bends the knees; Hanging_Pike hangs from a bar instead of pressing up on straight arms. Seated_Leg_Tucks and similar seated bench tucks sit on a bench and move dynamically. None shows a straight-arm support holding straight legs level.

rows.name: Weighted Decline Sit-Up
rows.reason: No candidate shows a decline sit-up with a free weight held at the chest for the whole rep. Press_Sit-Up adds an overhead barbell press, so it is a different movement. The band version uses band resistance, not a free weight (different implement). Decline_Crunch is unloaded and only a partial crunch. Otis-Up is weighted but on the floor and also presses overhead. Weighted_Crunches is a floor crunch. Sit-Up and 3/4 Sit-Up are on the floor and unweighted.

rows.name: Hollow-Body Hold
rows.reason: The source has no hollow-body hold: no entry name or instruction mentions 'hollow', and searching the instructions found nothing. Cocoons is a dynamic tuck crunch, not a static hold with the shoulders and straight legs off the floor. Dead Bug keeps the back flat but has the arms vertical and the limbs moving. Scissor Kick (arms out to the sides, legs alternating) and Flutter Kicks (prone on a bench) are different movements.

rows.name: Meadows Landmine Row
rows.reason: A Meadows row is a named variation. You stand perpendicular to the bar's end in a staggered stance, brace the non-working forearm on the front knee, grip the fat sleeve end overhand, and row with the elbow flared high toward the ceiling. None of the source photos show a perpendicular set-up, a staggered stance, a sleeve grip or a flared-elbow path. The single-arm long-bar rows are the base exercise, which the rules forbid using for a named variation.

rows.name: Landmine Squat
rows.reason: The movement is wrong. Landmine_Linear_Jammer is a squat plus press: frame 1 shows the arms locked out, so anyone copying it would do a thruster, not a squat. No other landmine source is a squat. Non-landmine squats (barbell back squat, goblet squat) fail on the implement.

rows.name: Landmine Hack Squat
rows.reason: The implement and movement are wrong. Barbell_Hack_Squat is a free barbell held behind the legs, and Hack_Squat is a machine. Neither is a landmine. Landmine_Linear_Jammer faces the anchor and adds a press.

rows.name: Landmine Reverse Lunge
rows.reason: The implement is wrong. Every reverse lunge in the source uses dumbbells, a barbell or bodyweight (Dumbbell_Rear_Lunge, Barbell_Lunge, Elevated_Back_Lunge), none of them a landmine. No landmine source shows a lunge.

rows.name: Landmine Lateral Lunge
rows.reason: The implement and movement are wrong. Barbell_Side_Split_Squat is a back-loaded free barbell, not a landmine. No landmine source shows a lateral lunge.

rows.name: Landmine Romanian Deadlift
rows.reason: The movement does not match. The long bar row is a row with a static hinge, never standing up. Copying it would train a row, not a hip hinge. The side deadlift uses an un-anchored barbell and is a squat-style suitcase lift, not an RDL. No source shows a landmine hinge.

rows.name: Landmine Single-Leg Romanian Deadlift
rows.reason: The source has no landmine single-leg hinge. The kettlebell one-legged deadlift has the right pattern but the wrong implement: it uses a kettlebell, not a barbell anchored at one end. The long-bar rows are rows from a two-leg stance, not single-leg RDLs. The other landmine sources (180s, Linear Jammer, Single-Arm Linear Jammer) are rotations or presses. A near miss on implement is not acceptable.

rows.name: Landmine Anti-Rotation Press
rows.reason: No source shows a landmine press that resists rotation. Landmine 180s is the opposite quality: the trunk deliberately rotates the bar 180 degrees and nothing is pressed. Both jammers are vertical or diagonal presses driven by the legs, one with a squat, and none shows the horizontal anti-rotation press-out. Pallof Press sources use a cable, so the implement is wrong.

rows.name: Landmine Clean and Press
rows.reason: No source shows the clean phase that lifts the landmine from the floor or hang to the shoulder. Both jammers start with the bar already at the shoulders, so they show only the press (with leg drive). That is the base press for a named variation the source lacks. Clean_and_Press and One-Arm_Kettlebell_Clean_and_Jerk use a free barbell or kettlebell, so the implement is wrong.

rows.name: Landmine Split Jerk
rows.reason: A split jerk needs the feet to split into a lunge catch under the locked-out bar. Neither landmine source shows a split. Their feet stay together or wide in both frames, so they are push presses or thrusters. Split_Jerk and One-Arm_Kettlebell_Split_Jerk show the split, but with a free barbell or a kettlebell, so the implement is wrong.

rows.name: Explosive Medicine-Ball Push-Up
rows.reason: The implement must be a medicine ball. The kettlebell crossover push-up has the same idea but the wrong implement (kettlebell handle grip versus hand on a ball). Drop_Push uses boxes. Plyo_Push-up and Clock_Push-Up are on the bare floor with no ball. Medicine-ball entries in the source (Chest Pass, Chest Push variants, Supine Chest Throw) are throws, not push-ups.

rows.name: Medicine-Ball Rotational Slam
rows.reason: A rotational slam is a two-hand slam that rotates the trunk and drives the ball into the floor beside the body, outside the foot. Both source slams are sagittal-plane overhead slams straight down in front, with no rotation, and one of them is single-arm. Medicine_Ball_Full_Twist is a back-to-back hand-off pass, not a slam. Copying any of these frames would teach a different movement, and no rotational slam exists in the source.

rows.name: Medicine-Ball Side Throw
rows.reason: A side throw is a ballistic scoop toss released sideways from the hip, with the athlete standing side-on to a partner or wall. The Full Twist is a slow back-to-back hand-off in which the ball is never thrown. Torso_Rotation is a stability-ball rotation stretch. The remaining source throws (Scoop Throw, Backward Throw, Overhead Throw, Chest Pass) are all sagittal-plane. The source has no side throw.

rows.name: Medicine-Ball Rotational Wall Throw
rows.reason: The app exercise needs a side-on stance and a throw driven by trunk rotation into a wall. No source exercise combines rotation with a throw. The wall chest push is a linear push from kneeling, and the twist photos involve no throw.

rows.name: Medicine-Ball Shot-Put Throw
rows.reason: A shot-put throw is a one-arm put of a medicine ball from the shoulder, driven by hip and trunk rotation. Heavy_Bag_Thrust uses a hanging heavy bag rather than a medicine ball, so nothing is released or thrown, which fails the implement rule. The chest-pass variants are two-handed and have no rotation, which fails the laterality and movement-pattern rules. The source has no shot-put throw.

rows.name: Half-Kneeling Rotational Throw
rows.reason: The app exercise needs a half-kneeling stance, trunk rotation and a ball throw. No source exercise has all three: the kneeling ball photos are two-knee linear chest pushes, and the rotational photos are standing hand-offs or stretches with no throw. Base exercises do not count for this named variation.

rows.name: Medicine-Ball Sprawl-to-Slam
rows.reason: A sprawl-to-slam joins a sprawl (dropping the hips and legs back to the floor, burpee-like) to a slam. Both source slams are standing-only, and nothing in the source shows a sprawl or burpee (keyword and instruction searches for sprawl or burpee find 0 hits). Using a plain slam would teach only half the movement and leave out the ground transition.

rows.name: Medicine-Ball Slam-to-Sprint
rows.reason: The app exercise is a slam that leads straight into a sprint. The source slams stay in place with no sprint start. Chest_Push_with_Run_Release does have a run-out, but it is a chest push, not a slam. No source exercise combines a slam with a sprint, so a slam-only photo would leave out the sprint.

rows.name: Weighted Box Jump
rows.reason: The only loaded box jump in the source starts seated from a bench, which is a separate named variation (Seated Box Jump), so its start position is wrong. The standing box jumps carry no load, and a 'Weighted' exercise needs a visible load. No source exercise shows a standing box jump with dumbbells or a vest.

rows.name: Single-Leg Broad Jump
rows.reason: A single-leg broad jump is one maximal-distance horizontal jump off one leg. Standing_Long_Jump is the two-leg base exercise, so its laterality is wrong. Single-Leg_Hop_Progression is a different drill: repeated low hops over cones rather than a maximal-distance jump, and the photos do not clearly show one leg. Single-Leg_Stride_Jump uses a box and a stride pattern. None is a true match.

rows.name: Pogo Jump
rows.reason: A pogo jump is an in-place, two-leg bounce driven by stiff ankles with no implement and no obstacle. Rope_Jumping adds a jump rope, a different implement and a different exercise. The cone hops travel forward over obstacles with knee tuck, which is a different pattern. Searches for pogo and ankle hops found nothing else.

rows.name: Zercher Carry
rows.reason: The Zercher hold is correct, but the source shows a squat, not a loaded carry. Someone copying the frames would squat instead of walking. The other carries in the source (Rickshaw_Carry, Farmer's Walk, Yoke_Walk) use different implements and holds. No source exercise shows walking with a barbell in the Zercher position.

rows.name: Cable Press Around
rows.reason: A cable press-around is a one-arm cable press that sweeps across and past the midline of the body. No source shows it. The cable chest presses are two-arm straight-line presses. Single-Arm_Cable_Crossover is a straight-arm fly from high pulleys. Around_The_Worlds is a dumbbell fly done in a circle. Each one differs in movement pattern, laterality or implement.

rows.name: Half-Kneeling Cable Chest Press
rows.reason: No source shows a cable chest press in a half-kneeling position. The available cable presses are standing, seated or on an incline bench, which is a body-position mismatch. They are also all two-arm, while the app describes this exercise as unilateral, trunk-controlled pressing. The only kneeling cable exercises in the source are rows, a crunch and a triceps extension, not chest presses.

rows.name: Cable Squeeze Press
rows.reason: In a squeeze press the handles are held together and squeezed against each other for the whole press. Every source cable press starts with the handles wide at the sides of the chest and only draws them partly together at lockout, so it is a standard cable chest press, not a squeeze press. Svend_Press is a squeeze press, but it uses plates, not cables, which is an implement mismatch.

rows.name: Cable Decline Press
rows.reason: The app's exercise is a downward-angled (high-to-low, decline) cable press with a braced trunk (catalog cue: 'downward pressing control and bracing'). No source photo shows a cable press on a downward line or on a decline bench. Cable_Chest_Press only mentions 'at an incline or decline' in its text, and its photo is a seated horizontal press. Standing_Cable_Chest_Press is horizontal. Incline_Cable_Chest_Press goes in the opposite direction. The only decline presses (Leverage_Decline_Chest_Press, Decline_Smith_Press, Decline_Barbell_Bench_Press, Decline_Dumbbell_Bench_Press) use a machine, Smith machine, barbell or dumbbells, not a cable.

rows.name: Single-Arm Cable Floor Press
rows.reason: The app's exercise needs a cable, one arm and a supine floor position. The source's floor presses (Floor_Press, One_Arm_Floor_Press, Dumbbell_Floor_Press, One-Arm_Kettlebell_Floor_Press, Alternating_Floor_Press, Leg-Over_Floor_Press) all use a barbell, dumbbell or kettlebell, which is the wrong implement. The cable presses are two-arm and not on the floor. No match is possible.

rows.name: Cable Resisted Push-Up
rows.reason: The implement and set-up are wrong for every candidate. The plain push-up has no cable load, so it is the base exercise without the named resistance. The cable presses are a different body position (upright or supine, not a prone push-up). Keyword searches for push, resist, cable and band found no resisted push-up.

rows.name: Cable Y Raise
rows.reason: A cable Y raise brings the arms up at about 30 degrees off the midline, usually to overhead, so the body makes a Y. The cables typically come from low pulleys. No cable photo shows this. The cable photos are a front raise, a lateral raise and a bent-over rear-delt raise, all stopping at shoulder height. Dumbbell_Scaption is the closest path, but it uses dumbbells instead of cables and stops at shoulder height instead of reaching a Y overhead.

rows.name: Cable Scaption Raise
rows.reason: Scaption is a thumbs-up raise in the scapular plane, about 30 degrees forward of the side. Neither cable source shows it: one is a frontal-plane lateral raise with a pronated, cross-body grip and the other a sagittal-plane front raise. Someone copying either would do a lateral or front raise, not scaption. The only true scaption photo (Dumbbell_Scaption) uses dumbbells, not a cable. No cable scaption or Y-raise exists in the source.

rows.name: Cable Cuban Rotation
rows.reason: A Cuban rotation is external rotation with the upper arm raised to shoulder height (90/90 scarecrow), with the forearm rotating from pointing forward or down to vertical. The cable photo shows external rotation with the elbow at the side, which is a different position and loads different parts of the range. Cuban_Press is the wrong implement (dumbbells) and adds an overhead press. The source has no cable 90/90 or Cuban rotation.

rows.name: Cable Serratus Punch
rows.reason: A serratus punch is a protraction-focused punch, usually one arm, that ends with the shoulder blade reaching forward past arm lockout. The only cable press photos are bilateral chest presses (standing, or seated for Cable_Chest_Press) that train pressing, not protraction. Laterality and movement emphasis both differ. The source has no cable punch or cable protraction exercise.

rows.name: Cable Standing Punch
rows.reason: The app's exercise is a single-arm, rotational, standing cable punch (qualities: power, rotation, unilateral). No source shows a single-arm cable punch with trunk rotation. Standing_Cable_Chest_Press is two-arm and has no rotation. Pallof presses are anti-rotation two-hand press-outs. Heavy_Bag_Thrust and the medicine-ball chest pushes are not cable. Using a two-arm press for a single-arm rotational punch is explicitly not acceptable.

rows.name: Cable Incline Press-Around
rows.reason: A press-around is a single-arm cable press that sweeps across the body toward the midline. The app's version is on an upward (incline) line with anti-rotation demand. No source photo shows a single-arm press-around, incline or otherwise. The incline cable press and incline fly are two-arm and use a different pattern (a straight press, or a fly). Single-Arm_Cable_Crossover is a fly on a high-to-low line. All of them fail on laterality, movement pattern or angle.

rows.name: Cable Front-Foot-Elevated Press
rows.reason: The app's exercise needs a split stance with the front foot elevated on a step or plate while pressing a cable. No source shows that stance. Standing_Cable_Chest_Press's text only says the stance may be staggered, its photo does not show the feet at all, and nothing is elevated. A plain standing cable press is the base exercise, not this named stance variation.

rows.name: Chest-Supported Cable Row
rows.reason: The source has no cable row with the chest supported. The chest-supported rows that exist use a lever machine (Lying_T-Bar_Row), dumbbells (Dumbbell_Incline_Row) or barbells (Lying_Cambered_Barbell_Row, Straight_Bar_Bench_Mid_Rows), so the implement is wrong. The cable rows are all free-torso seated, standing or kneeling rows.

rows.name: Rope Cable Row
rows.reason: A standard rope cable row pulls the rope to the lower chest or upper abdomen with the elbows travelling back along the torso, a lat and upper-back row. The only rope rows in the source are a rear-delt/high row to the neck with the arms abducted to 90 degrees, which takes the lats largely out of the movement, and a standing face pull. Copying either would teach a high row or face pull, not the app's row; the app lists a separate 'Cable High Row' for that pattern. The remaining seated cable rows use a V-handle or a single handle, not a rope.

rows.name: Cable Trap Raise
rows.reason: A 'trap raise' as coaches use the term is a trap-3 or Y-raise: an arm raise diagonally overhead in line with the lower-trap fibres. The app's secondary muscles (rear delts, rotator cuff) support this reading. The cable shrug is a different movement (pure elevation with no arm raise), and the bent-over cable lateral is a rear-delt raise perpendicular to the torso, not a Y or trap-3 path. The app's movement label 'Scapular elevation' leans toward a shrug, but the name says 'raise', not 'shrug'. When in doubt this is not a match. No cable Y-raise or trap-3 raise exists in the source.

rows.name: Cable High Pull
rows.reason: A high pull is an explosive pull driven by hip and knee extension, ending with the elbows high and wide. The app lists power and coordination, with glutes and quads as secondary muscles ('rapid whole-body arm-drive'). The only cable candidate is a strict, slow upright row with the torso held still and no lower-body drive. It is a close cousin, but someone copying the frames would do an upright row, not a high pull. Other high pulls in the source (Kettlebell_Sumo_High_Pull, barbell clean or snatch pulls) use the wrong implement.

rows.name: Incline Cable Curl
rows.reason: Incline Cable Curl means lying back on an incline bench and curling from a low pulley (arms hanging behind the torso). The only lying cable curl is flat on the floor, which is a different body position and shoulder angle, and every incline curl in the source uses free weights. Body position and implement can't both be right in any one photo.

rows.name: High Cable Curl
rows.reason: rejected variation: high cable curl is standing between pulleys; the photo is lying on a bench

rows.name: Cable Concentration Curl
rows.reason: The concentration-curl photos (seated, standing, barbell) all use free weights, which the rules rule out for a cable exercise. The only single-arm cable curl is a standing upright curl with no elbow-on-thigh brace, so it isn't a concentration curl. No source shows a cable concentration curl.

rows.name: Cable Spider Curl
rows.reason: A spider curl has the chest supported and the arms hanging free and vertical, with no pad under the upper arms. The source spider curl uses an EZ bar, not a cable, and the cable preacher curl rests the upper arms on the preacher pad, which makes it a preacher curl. Neither is a cable spider curl.

rows.name: Cross-Body Cable Curl
rows.reason: The only cross-body curl in the source uses a dumbbell, which isn't acceptable for a cable exercise. The single-arm cable curl goes straight up on the same side with a supinated grip, so it has neither the cross-body path nor the brachialis-focused neutral grip, and the rope hammer curl is two-arm and straight up. Nothing shows a cable curled across the body.

rows.name: Cross-Body Cable Triceps Extension
rows.reason: No source exercise shows a cross-body cable triceps extension, where the handle is taken from the opposite side and the elbow extends across or away from the body. The closest one, the single-arm pushdown, moves in a straight line down at the side. Copying it would give a single-arm pushdown, which the app already lists as #346 and which already uses that photo. The overhead and kneeling versions use a different plane and body position. The source instructions contain no cross-body triceps work.

rows.name: Cable Triceps Kickback
rows.reason: The implement is wrong: a dumbbell kickback is not a cable kickback. With dumbbells, gravity loads the arm in a different direction and there is no cable line. None of the cable triceps exercises use a bent-over posture with the upper arm parallel to the floor and the elbow extending backward. Searches for 'kickback' and for bent-over cable instructions found only a glute kickback (One-Legged_Cable_Kickback) and shoulder exercises.

rows.name: Cable Wrist Extension
rows.reason: Both cable wrist exercises use a supinated (palms-up) grip and train the wrist flexors. A wrist extension needs a palms-down grip and lifts the back of the hand. Copying these frames would train the opposite muscle group. The palms-down wrist curls in the source all use a dumbbell or barbell, which is the wrong implement for a cable exercise.

rows.name: Cable Belt Squat
rows.reason: There is no cable belt squat in the source. Weighted_Squat is a belt squat, but the load is a plate hanging from a dip belt, not a low-pulley cable attached to a belt, so the implement is wrong. Cable_Deadlifts uses cables, but the load is held in the hands on two handles at the sides, with no belt.

rows.name: Cable Goblet Squat
rows.reason: The source has no cable squat with a single handle held at the chest. Goblet_Squat uses a kettlebell (wrong implement). Cable_Deadlifts uses cables, but the handles hang at the sides (wrong hold and loading position). A keyword search for 'squat' among cable exercises returns 0 hits.

rows.name: Cable Front Squat
rows.reason: The source has no cable squat with the handles or bar held in a front-rack position. Its only cable squatting movement (Cable_Deadlifts) holds the handles at the sides. Front squats in the source (Front_Barbell_Squat, Front_Squat_Clean_Grip, Front_Squats_With_Two_Kettlebells) use barbells or kettlebells, not cables.

rows.name: Cable Good Morning
rows.reason: A good morning loads the upper back or chest while the athlete hinges. Pull_Through has the load in straight arms passing between the legs, which is a different exercise and has its own name. Band_Good_Morning has the right pattern but uses a band, not a cable. Cable_Deadlifts is a squat-style deadlift with handles at the sides. No source photo shows a cable good morning.

rows.name: Cable Single-Leg Deadlift
rows.reason: The single-leg hinge photo uses a kettlebell, which is the wrong implement for a cable exercise. Both cable hinge photos are two-leg, which is the wrong laterality. The source has no cable single-leg deadlift.

rows.name: Cable Step-Up
rows.reason: Every step-up in the source is loaded with dumbbells, a barbell or bodyweight (Step-up_with_Knee_Raise). None uses a cable, and a dumbbell or barbell version of a cable exercise is not acceptable.

rows.name: Cable Lateral Step-Up
rows.reason: The source has no cable exercise for the lower body that steps, lunges or squats. Searches for lunge, step and squat filtered to cable returned 0 hits, and a search of instructions mentioning cable or pulley turned up none either. Dumbbell_Step_Ups uses the wrong implement (dumbbells, not a cable) and the wrong direction (a forward step-up, not lateral). Barbell_Step_Ups has the same flaws. Single-Leg_High_Box_Squat is band-assisted, not loaded with a cable, and is not a step-up. Lateral_Box_Jump is a jump, not a step-up.

rows.name: Cable Skater Squat
rows.reason: In a skater squat the free knee travels behind the body, and the lift is loaded with a cable. Kettlebell_Pistol_Squat has the free leg in front and uses a kettlebell, so the movement and the implement are both wrong. Smith_Machine_Pistol_Squat and One_Leg_Barbell_Squat (rear foot elevated) are also different movements on different implements. Single-Leg_High_Box_Squat is band-assisted. The source has no cable squat of any kind.

rows.name: Cable Hip Thrust
rows.reason: A cable hip thrust is done on a bench with the shoulders supported and cable resistance at the hips. No source exercise is a cable thrust or bridge. Pull_Through has the same hip-extension aim, but the body position (standing) and the pattern differ. The barbell and band thrust or bridge versions use other implements. Their instructions rule them out, so their frames were not downloaded.

rows.name: Cable Quadruped Hip Extension
rows.reason: rejected variation: quadruped hip extension: the photo is a standing kickback

rows.name: Cable Donkey Kick
rows.reason: rejected variation: donkey kick is quadruped; the photo is a standing kickback

rows.name: Cable Fire Hydrant
rows.reason: A fire hydrant is quadruped hip abduction (the bent knee lifted out to the side) against cable resistance. The source has no cable quadruped abduction. The nearest photos differ in implement (bodyweight, machine), in direction (adduction), or in plane (extension). Hip_Circles_prone is a bodyweight stretch and was judged from its record.

rows.name: Cable Standing Hip Abduction
rows.reason: The source has no cable hip abduction. The only cable hip exercise, Cable_Hip_Adduction, moves the opposite way: the cuffed leg next to the stack comes in across the body against the cable. Abduction needs the far leg moving out, away from the stack. Band_Hip_Adductions uses a band, not a cable. Thigh_Abductor is a seated machine, not a standing cable exercise. Side_Leg_Raises and Standing_Hip_Circles are unloaded bodyweight drills.

rows.name: Cable Hamstring Curl
rows.reason: No source shows knee flexion against a cable. The only leg-and-ankle-cuff cable sources are the kickback (hip extension) and hip adduction. The curl sources are machines (Lying_Leg_Curls, Seated_Leg_Curl, Standing_Leg_Curl), a band (Seated_Band_Hamstring_Curl) or an exercise ball (Ball_Leg_Curl). The rules say a different implement is not a match.

rows.name: Cable Standing Leg Curl
rows.reason: Standing_Leg_Curl is the right movement but on a machine, not a cable, and the athlete is braced kneeling on the machine rather than standing free with an ankle cuff. One-Legged_Cable_Kickback is a cable and standing, but it shows hip extension with a straight knee, not a knee curl. Leg_Lift has no cable. No source shows a standing single-leg curl on a cable.

rows.name: Cable Leg Extension
rows.reason: The source's knee-extension exercises are all on a machine. No cable, ankle-cuff or low-pulley knee extension exists in the source, and I found no other cable lower-body source after listing every cable exercise. Machine is not cable.

rows.name: Cable Calf Raise
rows.reason: The implement is wrong for every candidate. A band, machine, Smith, barbell or dumbbell calf raise is not a cable calf raise, and the source has no cable-loaded plantarflexion photo.

rows.name: Cable Tibialis Raise
rows.reason: The source has no cable dorsiflexion exercise. The only dorsiflexion entry is the Smith machine reverse calf raise, which uses a different implement (Smith bar on the back, not a cable pulling on the foot) and a different set-up, and its frames do not clearly show the toes lifting. The other tibialis entries are a self-massage roll (Anterior_Tibialis-SMR) and a stretch (Posterior_Tibialis_Stretch), not raises. Searching the instructions for 'dorsi', 'tibialis' and 'toes toward shin' found nothing else.

rows.name: Cable Reverse Lunge
rows.reason: The movement pattern matches, but the implement does not. Dumbbell_Rear_Lunge uses dumbbells, not a cable, and the rules say a dumbbell version is not a cable exercise. Crossover_Reverse_Lunge is unloaded and adds a torso rotation. The source has no cable lunge.

rows.name: Cable Lateral Lunge
rows.reason: The movement is a lateral lunge, but the load is a back-squat barbell, not a cable. The implement differs, so it is not a match. The source has no cable lateral lunge.

rows.name: Cable Crossover Step Lunge
rows.reason: Only the name is similar. The source exercise is a mobility drill with no load and a straight-back step plus torso twist. It is not a diagonal crossover step resisted by a cable. Dumbbell_Rear_Lunge is a straight reverse lunge with dumbbells. The source has no cable or diagonal crossover lunge.

rows.name: Cable Forward March
rows.reason: A cable forward march is marching forward under resistance from a cable attached to a belt or harness, with the stack behind the athlete. The source has no cable march or cable-resisted gait. The closest, the harness sled drag, uses a different implement (sled) and is a sprint, not a march. The band hip flexion is a single knee raise on the spot with a band. Neither qualifies.

rows.name: Cable Standing Knee Drive
rows.reason: The band hip flexion photo has the right movement, but the app exercise names a cable, and the matching rules treat band and cable as different implements. The only cable photo with an ankle cuff (Cable Hip Adduction) is a frontal-plane adduction, not a knee drive. One-Legged Cable Kickback is hip extension. The source has no cable hip flexion or knee drive.

rows.name: Cable Dead Bug
rows.reason: The only dead bug in the source is bodyweight. The app exercise is a cable dead bug (cable tension pulling on the arms), and a bodyweight photo does not match the cable implement. There is no other dead bug entry.

rows.name: Cable Horizontal Chop
rows.reason: rejected variation: horizontal chop: the photo is a diagonal wood chop

rows.name: Cable Rotational Row
rows.reason: A cable rotational row is defined by deliberate trunk rotation during the pull: you turn toward the stack on the reach and rotate open as you row, and the obliques are prime movers. Shotgun Row is the nearest single-arm standing cable row, but its source instructions describe only shoulder retraction, elbow flexion and wrist supination, with no trunk rotation. The frames show a heavily hinged low-cable lat row in which any torso turn is incidental. Someone copying it would do a single-arm row, not a rotational row, so it is a near miss on the movement pattern (rotational vs straight). The seated one-arm row and the kneeling high-pulley row have no rotation and use the wrong position. No other cable row in the source shows rotation; Pallof Press With Rotation, Standing Cable Lift and Cable Russian Twists are presses or chops, not rows.

rows.name: Cable Anti-Rotation Walkout
rows.reason: An anti-rotation walkout means holding the cable handle in front of the chest and walking sideways away from the stack and back, resisting rotation while the tension rises. The only anti-rotation cable photos in the source are Pallof presses, a stationary press-out from the chest. That is a different movement (arm press, no walking), so it would be a near miss at best. No source exercise shows a walkout.

rows.name: Alternating Landmine Press
rows.reason: Alternating means passing or switching the bar between hands rep by rep. No source shows that. The single-arm jammer is a one-arm press with the same hand in both frames, plus leg drive. The two-handle jammer is simultaneous and bilateral, with a squat. Per the laterality rule, neither shows an alternating press.

rows.name: Tall-Kneeling Landmine Press
rows.reason: Body position must be tall-kneeling. Every landmine press photo in the source is standing with leg drive, so it fails on position. A search of all instructions for kneeling presses found only cable or bodyweight exercises (Kneeling Arm Drill, Kneeling Cable Triceps Extension), none of them landmine.

rows.name: Chest-Supported Landmine Row
rows.reason: The movement (a chest-supported two-arm T-bar row) is close, but the implement differs: the photo shows a dedicated T-bar row machine (source equipment 'machine', with its own frame, footplate and chest pad), not a landmine barbell set up with a bench. The rules list machine vs landmine as different implements, and someone copying the frames would need that machine. The app's own Chest-Supported T-Bar Row (#51) already uses this photo correctly. The other chest-supported rows in the source (Lying Cambered Barbell Row, Incline Bench Pull, Dumbbell Incline Row) are free-barbell or dumbbell rows on a bench, not landmine.

rows.name: Offset Landmine Row
rows.reason: 'Offset' is the defining word of this variation: an asymmetric or offset set-up such as a staggered/offset stance or an offset grip, built for anti-rotation. That is distinct from the plain single-arm landmine row, which is already matched to #256 with these photos. The source photos show a square-stance standard one-arm landmine row with nothing offset visible, and no source exercise names or shows an offset landmine row. Because the variation's defining element cannot be confirmed in any photo, using the base single-arm row would be a near miss.

rows.name: Landmine Split Press
rows.reason: This is the closest candidate: a one-arm standing landmine press. But the app name specifies a split stance (one foot well forward, one back, often with the rear knee bent), and the photo shows a wide or near-parallel stance with only a small stagger. It is also a push press with leg drive rather than a strict press. Under the stance rule this is a near miss, so the answer is none.

rows.name: Kettlebell Clean and Press
rows.reason: A clean and press needs both phases visible: a clean from a hang or the floor to the rack, then a strict press overhead. No kettlebell source photographs both. The one-arm clean-and-jerk frames stop at the rack, so they only teach the clean (the app already has 'Kettlebell Clean' on Kettlebell_Dead_Clean), and its finish would be a jerk, not a press. The press-only sources start at the rack with no clean, and the two-arm one is double-bell. Clean_and_Press exists only with a barbell (wrong implement).

rows.name: Lateral Goblet Squat
rows.reason: The source has no lateral squat with a goblet-held kettlebell. Barbell_Side_Split_Squat has the lateral pattern, but the load is a barbell on the back, not a goblet kettlebell. Goblet_Squat has the right implement and hold, but it is a symmetric bilateral squat with no lateral weight shift.

rows.name: Single-Leg Box Jump
rows.reason: A single-leg box jump takes off from one leg on the floor and lands on top of the box. Single_Leg_Push-off starts with the foot on the box and lands back on it, so the athlete never jumps onto the box. That is a different drill. Front_Box_Jump is two-leg (wrong laterality). Box_Skip and Single-Leg_Stride_Jump are alternating-leg bounding drills that leave the box. Single-Leg_Hop_Progression and Single-Leg_Lateral_Hop use cones with no box. None of them shows the exercise.

rows.name: Depth Drop to Stick
rows.reason: By name, a depth drop to stick means stepping off a box, landing and freezing in an athletic position. The two frames show exactly that: box, then landed position. They do not show the depth jump's rebound. The source is labelled 'Linear Depth Jump', but only its drop-and-land portion is photographed. Confidence is low for two reasons: (1) the app tags this exercise 'unilateral', and a single-leg landing would make this two-foot photo the wrong laterality, although the name does not say single-leg and the standard depth drop is bilateral; (2) frame 1 shows slight arm-motion blur, so the 'stick' is implied rather than clearly frozen. Depth_Jump_Leap shows a similar drop and landing but has a taller target box right in front, which signals a jump, and the app already uses it for 'Depth Jump'. If #394 is meant to be single-leg, the answer is none: no source shows a single-leg drop landing.

rows.name: Drop Landing
rows.review: Drop Landing: Linear_Depth_Jump frames show the step off and the landing, not the rebound.

rows.name: Assisted Nordic Hamstring Curl
rows.reason: Both are the standard, unassisted Nordic or natural glute-ham raise. Natural_Glute_Ham_Raise is already the app's photo for the base exercise (app id 192). Neither photo shows the assistance the name requires: no band supporting the torso, and no hands pushing off a box or the floor during the movement. The Natural frame-1 hand catch is the normal finish of an unassisted rep, and the partner in the Floor photos only anchors the ankles. Under the 'base exercise for a named variation' rule, this is not a match.

rows.name: Side Plank Hip Adduction
rows.reason: The app exercise is a side-plank variant that loads the adductors, with the bottom leg lifted up to the top leg or the top leg supported on a bench. Side_Bridge shows only a basic side plank with no adduction. Side_Leg_Raises is a standing leg swing. No source shows a side plank with adduction.

rows.name: Sled March
rows.reason: A sled march is a heavy sled push on high handles at a deliberate, marching tempo with knee drive. Implement (push sled), grip (high posts), body position (forward lean into the handles) and pattern (alternating-leg resisted gait) all match what the frames show. The only difference is tempo: the source is labelled a sprint and its instructions say to move as fast as possible. Tempo cannot be seen in a still, and nothing in the photo would teach a wrong position for a march. Confidence is low because the app already uses this same photo for 'Sled Sprint' and keeps 'Sled March' as a separate entry. A strict reviewer may count march versus sprint as a named variation the source lacks. Rejected alternatives: Sled_Push shows low-handle, near-horizontal pushing, already used for 'Heavy Sled Push'. Sled_Drag_-_Harness shows an upright harness sprint with running arm swing. Backward_Drag goes backwards with ropes.
